text: Welcome to Chapter Eight: PostgreSQL. We start with PL slash pgSQL versus T-SQL. The first structural difference you'll notice: where T-SQL's main unit is CREATE PROCEDURE, PostgreSQL leans on CREATE FUNCTION for almost everything procedural, even logic you'd naturally write as a stored procedure back in T-SQL.

Here's a function that totals a customer's orders. Create function, returns numeric, as dollar-dollar, declare a local variable, begin, select into it, return it, end, dollar-dollar, language plpgsql. That dollar-dollar wrapping the body is called dollar-quoting, and it's genuinely distinctive syntax.

Dollar-quoting solves a real problem: it lets you delimit the function body as a string without escaping single quotes used inside it. Write 'Hello, ' concatenated with name, unescaped, naturally. T-SQL never needs this trick in the first place, because a T-SQL procedure body isn't a quoted string literal at all.

Now the block structure itself: declare, begin, exception, end. This is worth naming directly — PL slash pgSQL and Oracle's PL slash SQL genuinely resemble each other more than either resembles T-SQL's looser, batch-based style, because PostgreSQL's procedural language was deliberately modeled on Oracle's.
And calling it is different too. Select get_customer_total, 42, in parentheses — called like any ordinary expression inside a SELECT, not with T-SQL's EXEC keyword.

FUNCTION instead of PROCEDURE for most things, dollar-quoting instead of escaped strings, and a block structure borrowed from Oracle rather than T-SQL. Next lesson: PostgreSQL's genuinely native array and JSONB types. See you there.
